topic_info.title: Incision and drainage of skin abscess (procedure)

editor.editor_institution: Department of Family Medicine, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

list.listitem: Drainage of a carbuncle, furuncle, and other skin abscess (a localized collection of purulence).

Equipment: Local anesthetic of choice (usually 1% or 2% lidocaine with or without epinephrine). A syringe of 3 cc with 25- to 30-gauge needle. Number 11 or 15 retractable scalpel blade. Small curved hemostat. Dressing supplies. Optional: Packing material, culture material, suturing supplies.

Incision and drainage starts with selection of the wound to drain. There are no absolute contraindications to an incision and drainage (I&D), though large or deep abscesses near the eyes or other vital structures require more care to avoid complications and may be an indication for referral. The physician should feel for softness under the suspected abscess that indicates purulence. If there is doubt about the existence of purulence, perform a needle aspiration.

Use 1% or 2% lidocaine with or without epinephrine for local anesthesia. Because of the acidic environment of an abscess, adequate anesthesia may be difficult to obtain. A field block technique may be used instead of direct infiltration.

This is not a strictly sterile procedure; as the goal is to drain infected material, a sterile field is not mandatory. Abscesses can be under considerable pressure, so eye and mucous membrane protection for the operator is recommended to protect against inadvertent splatter. If excess pressure is suspected, initial drainage with an 18-gauge needle can prevent squirting.

After the skin is anesthetized, a stab wound is made with the scalpel at 90° to the skin. The scalpel or a hemostat can be used to break up loculations and help drain puss. Squeezing out the purulence is painful, but may be necessary in order to remove all the purulence.
The wound can be sutured, left open to drain, or packed.

Loop drainage technique (LDT): A meta-analysis of 8 studies involving 910 patients found that conventional I&D is more likely than the newer loop drainage technique (LDT) to lead to treatment failure of abscesses (OR 2.02, 95% CI 1.29-3.18). LDT is performed by creating two small incisions at opposite poles of the abscess, using small forceps to break loculations through these two incisions, then inserting a "vessel loop" and tying it over the skin surface to facilitate continued drainage, thereby avoiding the need for packing and minimizing postoperative visits. Some prefabricated silicone vessel loops do not even require tying or suturing.

Routine wound culture is controversial. Physicians must determine the likelihood for the presence of an unusual infection or for specific antibiotic resistance. If uncertainty exists, obtaining a culture is reasonable but may not be helpful. The culture should be taken from the abscess cavity, not the surrounding skin.

Routine use of antimicrobial agents after the I&D is similarly controversial. A retrospective cohort study found a small benefit to antibiotics in patients with community-acquired methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (CA-MRSA) (95% vs 87% clinical cure). However, a prospective double-blinded RCT in 166 adults (65% CA-MRSA) found no benefit to antibiotics (90% clinical cure with placebo, 84% with cephalexin). Similarly, a recent RCT in 161 children found no benefit to antibiotics. However, a RCT of 786 adults and children with superficial small (<5 cm) abscesses found slightly fewer treatment failures (NNT = 7) when clindamycin or TMP/SMX were prescribed after incision and drainage.

Many physicians will treat patients that have large areas of cellulitis, those with systemic symptoms such as fever or chills, with extensive tissue involvement, or with abscess in the nasal region with an antibiotic. While this seems prudent, there are no studies for or against this practice.
Most skin abscesses resolve without sequelae. Hospitalization may be required for large areas of cellulitis, failure of outpatient treatment, or for immunocompromised patients.
If systemic symptoms such as a high fever are present, systemic antibiotics or further evaluation may be warranted.
Although good evidence is lacking, it is reasonable to obtain a fasting blood sugar and ask about drug use when a patient has had recurrent skin abscesses.
Wounds should be reevaluated in 2 to 3 days, and culture results reviewed and acted on if these were obtained.
If cultures were not obtained, evaluation for improvement is necessary in the event of treatment failure.
In the event that cultures are positive for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), routine evaluation for a MRSA carrier state (ie, nasal swabs) is not recommended.
CPT codes vary by site and the complexity of the procedure. A CPT manual should be consulted for proper billing.
Typical fees for this procedure vary with the site and complexity.
Patients may return to work as soon as they feel well enough to do so and they can perform their job duties, with the following caveats:

A MRSA infection should not routinely exclude return to work. Exclusion from work should be reserved for those with wound drainage ("pus") that cannot be covered and contained with a clean, dry bandage and for those who cannot maintain good hygiene practices.
Workers with active infections should be excluded from activities where skin-to-skin contact with the affected skin area is likely to occur until their infections are healed.
Healthcare workers should discuss return to work issues with their infection control personnel.
